questions.q: What is meant by the diffraction of a waveform as it passes a barrier or through a small opening?
options: The bending of the wave towards the normal as it slows down in a denser medium
The spreading out of the wave as it passes a barrier or passes through a small opening
The cancelling of two waves to produce a region of no displacement
The splitting of white light into its separate colours by a prism
questions.explanation: Diffraction of a waveform is the spreading out of that wave when it passes a barrier or passes through a small opening. The episode uses the same definition as Link one of the chain: diffraction is the prerequisite spreading that lets the two slits' waves overlap at all.

questions.q: Why is the diffraction of light much more difficult to observe than the diffraction of water waves?
options: Light travels too fast for the spreading to be seen by eye
Water waves carry far more energy than light waves
The size of the opening or barrier must be similar to the wavelength of the wave, and light's wavelength is far smaller than that of water waves
Light cannot diffract around a barrier at all, only water waves can
questions.explanation: Diffraction is only significant when the size of the opening or barrier is similar to the wavelength of the wave. Water waves have much longer wavelengths, so their diffraction is easy to see, whereas light's wavelength is only a few hundred nanometres, which is exactly why the slits in Young's experiment must be microscopically narrow.

questions.q: State Huygens's Principle, and explain how it accounts for a wavefront fanning out through a gap in a barrier.
keyPoints: Every point on a wavefront acts as a source of circular secondary wavelets that travel in the direction of the wave.
The new wavefront is the surface tangential to (the envelope of) all those wavelets.
When a barrier blocks part of the wave, not all the point sources contribute, so the wavefront at the edge forms a circular shape that fans out — this is diffraction.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that each point on a wavefront re-radiates as a secondary wavelet, that the new wavefront is their envelope, and that a blocking barrier leaves the edge free to fan out, grade yourself Good or Easy. In the episode this is the engine under both diffraction and the two slits acting as fresh point sources.

questions.q: In Young's experiment the light from the two pinholes is described as coherent. What does coherent mean, and how did Young achieve it?
options: The two sources are very bright; achieved by using a powerful lamp
The two sources are monochromatic and in phase; achieved by illuminating both pinholes with one wavefront from a single source
The two sources have different wavelengths; achieved by using two separate coloured lamps
The two sources are polarised at right angles; achieved with a polarising filter
questions.explanation: Coherent means the sources are monochromatic and in phase. Young deliberately used just one source so that a single wavefront arrived at both pinholes, keeping the two emerging waves synchronised. Two separate lamps would be incoherent, with a random phase relationship and no discernible pattern on the screen.

questions.q: In terms of the path difference between the two pinholes, what are the conditions for a bright band (constructive interference) and a dark band (destructive interference) on the screen?
options: Bright when the path difference is \((n-0.5)\lambda\); dark when it is \(n\lambda\)
Bright when the path difference is a whole number multiple of the wavelength, \(n\lambda\); dark when it is \((n-0.5)\lambda\)
Bright and dark both occur only when the path difference is exactly zero
Bright when the path difference is \(n\lambda\); dark when it is also \(n\lambda\)
questions.explanation: Constructive interference (a bright band) occurs when the path difference is a whole number multiple of the wavelength, \(n\lambda\), so the waves are in phase. Destructive interference (a dark band) occurs when the path difference is \((n-0.5)\lambda\), so crests meet troughs exactly out of phase and cancel. The episode's hook for this is "whole is bright, half is dark."

questions.q: Using the path difference between the two slits, account for the formation of the bright and dark bands when monochromatic light passes through a double slit. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Waves reach a given point on the screen along two alternative routes, one through each slit, and the difference between the lengths of these two paths is the path difference. Where the path difference is a whole number multiple of the wavelength (\(n\lambda\)) the waves arrive in phase, crests reinforce crests, and constructive interference produces a bright band. Where the path difference is \((n-0.5)\lambda\) the crests of one wave always meet the troughs of the other, so the waves are exactly out of phase, destructive interference occurs, and that place on the screen is a dark band. Because both slits are illuminated by the same wavefront the two waves are coherent, so the pattern of maxima and minima is stable.

criteria.descriptor: Defines path difference as the difference in distance travelled from the two slits to a point on the screen.
Bright band: path difference = \(n\lambda\), waves in phase, constructive interference.
Dark band: path difference = \((n-0.5)\lambda\), waves out of phase, destructive interference.
Notes the two slits are coherent (lit by the same wavefront), giving a stable pattern.

questions.explanation: This is the spine of the episode ("Dogs Chase Other Cats Daily"). The marks live in tying each path-difference condition to in-phase/out-of-phase and naming constructive vs destructive interference.

questions.q: A sodium lamp produces almost-monochromatic light of wavelength 589 nm. It falls on parallel slits 0.100 mm apart and forms an interference pattern on a screen 1.50 m away. Determine the angle to the first-order maximum and the distance of that maximum from the central maximum on the screen.
questions.explanation: Straight application of \(d\sin\theta = m\lambda\) with \(m = 1\), then \(x = L\sin\theta\) because the angle is tiny. The small angle (0.337°) shows the fringes sit very close to the central axis, and since the maxima are evenly spaced the third-order maximum is simply \(3\times8.8 = 26.4\,\mathrm{mm}\) out.

questions.q: White light falls on slits of separation 10 μm. For red light of wavelength 700 nm, determine the angle of the first-order maximum, and show why red is dispersed to a larger angle than blue light.
working: Red has the longer wavelength, so for the same slit separation \(d\) it gives the larger diffracting angle.
questions.explanation: Because \(\theta\) increases with \(\lambda\), each colour in white light is sent to a slightly different angle, so each maximum is dispersed into a small spectrum running from blue out to red. Only the central maximum, where the path difference is zero for every colour, stays white.

questions.q: From memory, name the five links in the cause-and-effect chain the episode uses (mnemonic 'Dogs Chase Other Cats Daily') that builds the double-slit pattern from scratch.
keyPoints: Diffraction — each narrow slit spreads the light out because the gap is comparable to the wavelength.
Coherence — both slits are lit by one wavefront, so they act as coherent secondary sources (same wavelength, constant phase).
Overlap — the two diffracted waves overlap on the screen and superpose.
Constructive — where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths the waves are in phase and reinforce: a bright band.
Destructive — where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths plus a half the waves are out of phase and cancel: a dark band.
questions.explanation: Each link is a separate marking point. If you produced all five (Diffraction, Coherence, Overlap, Constructive, Destructive) and tied the last two to path difference and phase, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Why is the appearance of dark bands the decisive evidence that light behaves as a wave rather than a stream of particles?
options: Dark bands prove that the light is reflected straight back by the slits
At a dark band, light arriving from both slits combines to produce darkness — particles could only ever add to give more light, but waves can cancel by destructive interference
Dark bands show that the slits absorb some of the incoming light particles
Dark bands appear only when the light is polarised, which is a particle property
questions.explanation: A dark band is a place where light from both slits arrives yet the result is darkness — light plus light giving no light. Particles (corpuscles) could only ever pile up to give more light, never cancel; only waves, with crests and troughs, can interfere destructively to zero. That is why the double-slit pattern is the headline evidence for the wave model. (The experiment shows light is a wave, but not that it is transverse — that needs polarisation.)
